This practice guidance was approved by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases on June 15, 2017. Preamble This guidance provides a data‐supported approach to the diagnostic, therapeutic, and preventive aspects of nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD) care. A “Guidance” document is different from a “Guideline.” Guidelines are developed by a multidisciplinary panel of experts and rate the quality (level) of the evidence and the strength of each recommendation using the Grading of Recommendations, Assessment Development, and Evaluation system. A guidance document is developed by a panel of experts in the topic, and guidance statements, not recommendations, are put forward to help clinicians understand and implement the most recent evidence. This Practice Guidance was commissioned by the American Association for the Study of Liver Diseases (AASLD) and is an update to the Practice Guideline published in 2012 in conjunction with the American Gastroenterology Association and the American College of Gastroenterology (ACG).1 Sections where there have been no notable newer publications are not modified, so some paragraphs remain unchanged. This narrative review and guidance statements are based on the following: (1) a formal review and analysis of the recently published world literature on the topic (Medline search up to August 2016); (2) the American College of Physicians' Manual for Assessing Health Practices and Designing Practice Guidelines2; (3) guideline policies of the AASLD; and (4) the experience of the authors and independent reviewers with regard to NAFLD. This practice guidance is intended for use by physicians and other health professionals. As clinically appropriate, guidance statements should be tailored for individual patients. Specific guidance statements are evidence based whenever possible, and, when such evidence is not available or is inconsistent, guidance statements are made based on the consensus opinion of the authors.3 This is a practice guidance for clinicians rather than a review article, and interested readers can refer to several recent comprehensive reviews.4 Because this guidance document is lengthy, to make it easier for the reader, a list of all guidance statements and recommendations are provided in a tabular form as Supporting Table S1. Definitions For defining NAFLD, there must be (1) evidence of hepatic steatosis (HS), either by imaging or histology, and (2) lack of secondary causes of hepatic fat accumulation such as significant alcohol consumption, long‐term use of a steatogenic medication, or monogenic hereditary disorders (Table 1). In the majority of patients, NAFLD is commonly associated with metabolic comorbidities such as obesity, diabetes mellitus, and dyslipidemia. NAFLD can be categorized histologically into nonalcoholic fatty liver (NAFL) or nonalcoholic steatohepatitis (NASH; Table 2). NAFL is defined as the presence of ≥5% HS without evidence of hepatocellular injury in the form of hepatocyte ballooning. NASH is defined as the presence of ≥5% HS and inflammation with hepatocyte injury (e.g., ballooning), with or without any fibrosis. For defining “advanced” fibrosis, this guidance document will be referring specifically to stages 3 or 4, that is, bridging fibrosis or cirrhosis. claims.text: NAFL is defined as the presence of at least 5% hepatic steatosis without evidence of hepatocellular injury in the form of hepatocyte ballooning.
NASH is defined as the presence of at least 5% hepatic steatosis with inflammation and hepatocyte injury, with or without fibrosis.
Advanced fibrosis in NAFLD refers specifically to stage 3 bridging fibrosis or stage 4 cirrhosis.
Weight loss of 7% to 10% is required to improve key histological parameters of NASH including liver fibrosis.
Pioglitazone improves liver histology in patients with biopsy-proven NASH both with and without type 2 diabetes.
Vitamin E administered at a daily dose of 800 IU/day improves liver histology in non-diabetic adults with biopsy-proven NASH.
Statins can be safely used to treat dyslipidemia in patients with NAFLD or NASH.
Metformin is not recommended as a specific treatment for liver disease in patients with NASH.
Omega-3 fatty acids are not recommended as a specific treatment for NAFLD or NASH.
Bariatric surgery is not recommended as a primary treatment for NASH.

limitations.text: Where high-level clinical trial evidence is lacking or inconsistent, guidance statements rely on author consensus opinion.
Long-term clinical efficacy and safety of pioglitazone and vitamin E in patients with NASH remain unproven.
Noninvasive tools like transient elastography have higher failure rates in severely obese patients and cannot reliably distinguish NAFL from NASH.

future_work.text: Long-term randomized clinical trials evaluating pharmacologic agents specifically targeting hepatic fibrosis and NASH resolution.
Validation of noninvasive diagnostic tools and biomarkers capable of differentiating NAFL from NASH.

methodologies.name: AASLD Practice Guidance Narrative Review
methodologies.description: A systematic synthesis of Medline literature through August 2016 combined with ACP manual guidelines and expert author consensus to formulate clinical guidance statements for NAFLD care.
conditions: Patients with nonalcoholic fatty liver disease (NAFLD)
